explanation: The population at risk must only include disease-free individuals capable of developing the new condition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h1)

question: Prevalence differs from incidence because prevalence measures which of the following?

options.A: All existing cases at a specific time
options.B: The rate of recovery from an infection
options.C: Total deaths caused by an outbreak
options.D: Only newly diagnosed cases in a year

explanation: Prevalence captures the total burden by counting both old and existing cases together at one moment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h2)

question: A community clinic plans resource allocation for long-term care of diabetic patients. Which metric is most useful?

options.A: Disease prevalence
options.B: Case fatality rate
options.C: Disease incidence
options.D: Attack rate

explanation: Prevalence shows the total number of people living with a condition, helping plan ongoing care and drug supplies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h2)

question: What value is multiplied by the fraction to express incidence per standard population size?

options.A: The average age of the affected patients
options.B: A base factor like 1,000 or 100,000
options.C: The total number of hospital beds available
options.D: The total number of recovered individuals

explanation: Multiplying by a factor like 1,000 or 100,000 standardizes the figure for clear reporting and comparison. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h3)

question: What happens to the incidence rate if individuals in the denominator already have the disease?

options.A: The calculation remains completely accurate
options.B: The time factor is automatically doubled
options.C: The rate becomes artificially lowered
options.D: The rate becomes artificially elevated

explanation: Including immune or already-sick people in the denominator wrongly increases the population at risk, deflating the rate. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h3)

question: Cumulative incidence assumes that every person in the study group is followed for what duration?

options.A: The entire specified time period
options.B: Until they migrate out of the country
options.C: Until they develop a secondary illness
options.D: Only the first few days of life

explanation: Cumulative incidence requires complete follow-up of all participants across the full duration of observation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h4)

question: When is incidence density preferred over cumulative incidence in public health research?

options.A: When studying non-infectious chronic conditions exclusively
options.B: When the researcher wants to measure total existing cases
options.C: When study participants enter or leave at different times
options.D: When every single patient stays in the study until the end

explanation: Incidence density uses person-time denominators to handle loss to follow-up or migration in dynamic populations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h4)

question: Which factor directly drives down the incidence of vaccine-preventable diseases in a community?

options.A: Mass immunization campaigns
options.B: High population density
options.C: Heavy seasonal rainfall
options.D: Poor environmental sanitation

explanation: Immunization builds community immunity, preventing susceptible individuals from contracting and spreading infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h5)

question: Why does increased seasonal rainfall often lead to a spike in malaria incidence in Nigeria?

options.A: It lowers the nutritional status of rural farmers
options.B: It forces people to crowd into closed indoor spaces
options.C: It washes away essential community medication stocks
options.D: It creates breeding sites for mosquito vectors

explanation: Standing water pools from heavy rains provide ideal environments for mosquitoes to multiply and transmit malaria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h5)

question: What is the primary public health purpose of monitoring weekly disease incidence?

options.A: Detecting outbreaks early to trigger rapid responses
options.B: Calculating total historical healthcare costs
options.C: Determining total population growth rates
options.D: Assessing individual patient recovery speeds

explanation: Monitoring new cases week by week allows health teams to spot unusual clustering and stop outbreaks early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h6)

question: How do public health nurses use incidence trends over several years?

options.A: To set pharmaceutical drug prices in local markets
options.B: To evaluate the success of disease control programs
options.C: To diagnose individual patients reporting to the clinic
options.D: To determine daily staff shift rosters in the ward

explanation: Comparing yearly incidence curves shows whether public health interventions are successfully reducing disease transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h6)

question: Which Nigerian health workers are frontline reporters for new disease cases in communities?

options.A: National pharmaceutical manufacturing managers
options.B: Nurses and community health extension workers
options.C: University medical laboratory researchers
options.D: Hospital administrative accountants and cashiers

explanation: Nurses and CHEWs staff primary health centres and spot new cases during routine patient consultations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h7)

question: A primary health centre in a rural Nigerian LGA notes a sudden rise in suspected cholera cases. What immediate action should follow?

options.A: Transfer all health personnel to urban tertiary hospitals
options.B: Report the incidence data upward to trigger rapid response teams
options.C: Stop recording patient visits to reduce administrative workload
options.D: Wait until the end of the year to publish a formal report

explanation: Prompt reporting of new cases ensures higher health authorities deploy aid and containment measures immediately. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h7)

question: What defines a communicable disease?

options.A: An illness passed from an infected source to a susceptible host
options.B: A sudden injury resulting from physical trauma in the environment
options.C: A chronic condition caused by genetic mutation and lifestyle
options.D: A non-infectious metabolic disorder of the endocrine system

explanation: Communicable diseases are characterized by their ability to spread from one person or reservoir to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h1)

question: Which category of pathogen causes malaria?

options.A: Parasite
options.B: Fungus
options.C: Virus
options.D: Bacterium

explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species, which are microscopic parasites transmitted by mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h1)

question: An unexpected rise in cholera cases in a single state is classified as what?

options.A: An endemic
options.B: A pandemic
options.C: A sporadic event
options.D: An epidemic

explanation: An epidemic describes a sudden surge of cases exceeding the normal baseline expected in a specific region. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h2)

question: What term describes the constant presence of a disease in a specific region?

options.A: Epidemic
options.B: Pandemic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Incidence

explanation: An endemic disease is regularly found and maintained within a particular geographic area without spiking drastically. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h2)

question: Applying hand sanitizer breaks which specific link in the chain of infection?

options.A: Susceptible host
options.B: Mode of transmission
options.C: Infectious agent
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: Hand hygiene removes pathogens from the hands, stopping them from moving from one surface or person to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h3)

question: What represents a portal of exit for respiratory infections?

options.A: Intact epidermal skin layers
options.B: Respiratory secretions from coughing
options.C: Normal resting heart rate
options.D: Stable blood pressure readings

explanation: Respiratory droplets expelled through coughing or sneezing serve as the primary exit route for airborne pathogens. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h3)

question: A patient contracts malaria after being bitten by a mosquito. What transmission type is this?

options.A: Direct contact transmission
options.B: Airborne transmission
options.C: Vehicle-borne transmission
options.D: Vector-borne transmission

explanation: Mosquitoes act as living vectors that carry the parasite from an infected host to a new person. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h4)

question: Sharing an unwashed drinking cup with a typhoid patient demonstrates which transmission route?

options.A: Airborne transmission
options.B: Indirect transmission
options.C: Direct transmission
options.D: Vector-borne transmission

explanation: Contaminated objects like cups act as vehicles or fomites that indirectly pass pathogens to a new host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h4)

question: What is the primary animal reservoir for the Lassa fever virus in Nigeria?

options.A: Pond-dwelling frog
options.B: Free-roaming cattle
options.C: Multi-mammate rat
options.D: Domestic stray dog

explanation: The Mastomys rat serves as the natural host and reservoir for the Lassa virus, shedding the virus in its urine and droppings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h5)

question: Which clinical sign is most characteristic of severe cholera infection?

options.A: Rapid dehydration from watery diarrhea
options.B: Painful swelling of the parotid glands
options.C: Itchy skin rashes on the trunk
options.D: Chronic productive cough with blood

explanation: Cholera toxin causes profuse watery diarrhea that quickly leads to severe fluid loss and hypovolemic shock. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h5)

question: Why is early diagnostic confirmation of a communicable disease vital for public health?

options.A: It guarantees the patient will develop lifelong natural immunity
options.B: It removes all requirements for supportive intravenous fluid therapy
options.C: It triggers prompt epidemiological reporting to prevent outbreaks
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any barrier nursing care

explanation: Identifying cases quickly allows health authorities to track trends and implement containment measures before infections spread widely. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h6)

question: Which bedside tool is commonly used for quick screening of malaria in primary clinics?

options.A: Pulmonary spirometry meter
options.B: Rapid diagnostic test kit
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Electrocardiogram machine

explanation: Rapid diagnostic tests provide quick detection of malaria parasite antigens from a finger-prick blood sample. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of high routine immunization coverage in a community?

options.A: Removing the need for hand hygiene in hospitals
options.B: Completely eradicating all known bacteria from the soil
options.C: Building herd immunity to protect vulnerable populations
options.D: Ensuring zero hospital admissions for physical trauma

explanation: Widespread vaccination creates herd immunity, shielding individuals who cannot be vaccinated due to age or medical reasons. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h7)

question: Which measure is classified as an environmental sanitation control against disease?

options.A: Providing access to safe, clean drinking water
options.B: Inspecting surgical instruments for rust damage
options.C: Performing routine blood pressure screening tests
options.D: Administering therapeutic antibiotics to a patient

explanation: Clean water supplies prevent the fecal-oral transmission of pathogens that cause waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h7)

question: A community health nurse notices a cluster of measles cases. What immediate action should be taken?

options.A: Advise families to stay indoors and stop seeking all medical attention
options.B: Prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics to every healthy person in the town
options.C: Close the local primary health center permanently until further notice
options.D: Report the cluster to public health authorities and initiate contact tracing

explanation: Timely reporting and contact tracing help contain the spread of highly contagious viral infections in communities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h8)

question: What practice helps nurses prevent accidental needle-stick injuries in clinical settings?

options.A: Storing used needles openly on procedure trolleys
options.B: Recapping used injection needles before disposal
options.C: Using proper waste segregation and safety boxes
options.D: Washing contaminated syringes with cold tap water

explanation: Disposing of sharps immediately into puncture-resistant safety boxes protects healthcare workers from bloodborne infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h8)

question: What defines an endemic disease in a population?

options.A: Constant and predictable presence in a specific area
options.B: Rapid increase in cases over a short period
options.C: Sudden spread across multiple continents worldwide
options.D: Total absence of the disease for several years

explanation: Endemic diseases persist at a steady baseline rate within a defined geographic location over long periods. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h1)

question: Why is knowing the baseline rate of an endemic disease important for nurses?

options.A: It helps identify when normal case numbers begin to spike.
options.B: It guarantees the total eradication of the infection.
options.C: It ensures that vaccination programs are no longer needed.
options.D: It proves that the community has complete immunity.

explanation: Tracking the constant baseline allows healthcare workers to spot unusual surges that signal an outbreak. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h1)

question: An unexpected surge of disease cases in a specific community is called what?

options.A: A pandemic
options.B: An endemic
options.C: A syndrome
options.D: An epidemic

explanation: An epidemic represents a sudden spike above the normal expected baseline within a specific population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h2)

question: What main feature separates a pandemic from an epidemic?

options.A: Global spread across multiple countries and continents
options.B: Strictly seasonal occurrence during the rainy months
options.C: Restriction to a single rural village or town
options.D: A lower mortality rate among infected patients

explanation: While an epidemic is localized or regional, a pandemic crosses international borders to affect multiple continents. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h2)

question: What are the three components of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Prevention, cure, and palliation
options.B: Vector, treatment, and recovery
options.C: Agent, host, and environment
options.D: Bacterium, virus, and fungus

explanation: The classic epidemiological model evaluates the interaction between the infectious agent, the susceptible host, and the surrounding environment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h3)

question: Standing water near residential houses allows mosquitoes to breed. Which part of the epidemiological triangle does this represent?

options.A: The environment
options.B: The agent
options.C: The immunity
options.D: The host

explanation: External physical surroundings that facilitate vector breeding and disease transmission are classified under environmental factors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h3)

question: Which vector transmits the parasite responsible for endemic malaria?

options.A: Multimammate rat
options.B: Tsetse fly
options.C: Housefly
options.D: Female Anopheles mosquito

explanation: Plasmodium parasites are transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h4)

question: Which animal serves as the natural reservoir host for the Lassa virus?

options.A: Brown stray dog
options.B: Bovine cattle
options.C: Multimammate rat
options.D: Domestic pig

explanation: Lassa fever is a zoonotic illness spread primarily through contact with the excreta of the multimammate rat. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h4)

question: Why do waterborne infections remain endemic in communities with poor infrastructure?

options.A: Lack of electricity prevents the local hospital from storing drugs.
options.B: Continuous exposure to contaminated water sources maintains transmission cycles.
options.C: High environmental temperatures cause bacteria to multiply inside the human body.
options.D: Infected individuals develop permanent immunity after the first week.

explanation: When clean water is absent, people repeatedly ingest pathogens, sustaining the endemic cycle within the community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h5)

question: Which factor directly contributes to the constant presence of vector-borne diseases in tropical regions?

options.A: High uptake of routine childhood immunizations
options.B: Widespread availability of piped indoor plumbing
options.C: High humidity and favorable rainfall patterns
options.D: Strict enforcement of local sanitation laws

explanation: Favorable tropical climates provide optimal breeding habitats for mosquitoes and other disease vectors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in a primary health clinic?

options.A: To replace the need for laboratory diagnostic testing
options.B: To punish communities that fail to maintain clean environments
options.C: To guarantee funding from international health organizations
options.D: To detect unusual changes in disease frequency and patterns

explanation: Surveillance allows nurses to spot abnormal increases in disease rates so interventions can start immediately. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h6)

question: A clinic nurse notices an unusual rise in patients presenting with watery diarrhea over three days. What action should the nurse take next?

options.A: Report the cluster to local public health surveillance officers
options.B: Close the clinic until the infection clears up on its own
options.C: Wait until the end of the month to review the statistics
options.D: Advise patients to stop drinking local water without testing it

explanation: Prompt reporting of unusual disease clusters is a core responsibility of the nurse in disease monitoring. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h6)

question: A community health nurse distributes insecticide-treated nets to pregnant mothers in a rural village. Which control strategy is being applied?

options.A: Vector control and prevention of bites
options.B: Eradication of the infectious agent reservoir
options.C: Treatment of active clinical infections
options.D: Improvement of municipal water supplies

explanation: Insecticide-treated nets create a physical and chemical barrier against mosquitoes, reducing transmission of vector-borne illnesses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h7)

question: Why is health education considered vital in managing endemic conditions?

options.A: It empowers community members to adopt protective daily habits.
options.B: It completely eliminates all disease-causing vectors overnight.
options.C: It replaces the need for medical treatments and drugs.
options.D: It ensures patients never contract any infection again.

explanation: Educating the public fosters sustainable behavioral changes, such as handwashing and net usage, that lower infection risks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h7)

question: What term describes the constant presence of a disease within a specific geographic area?

options.A: Epidemic
options.B: Pandemic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Outbreak

explanation: An endemic disease remains constantly present at a baseline level within a particular region or population group. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h1)

question: An unexpected rise of cholera cases in a single rural community is best classified as what?

options.A: An endemic
options.B: A pandemic
options.C: An outbreak
options.D: A non-communicable condition

explanation: An outbreak refers to a localized surge of disease cases in a restricted geographic setting or community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h1)

question: The virus or bacterium that causes an infectious disease is known as what component of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Vector
options.B: Host
options.C: Agent
options.D: Environment

explanation: The agent is the specific biological pathogen, such as a bacterium or virus, responsible for causing the illness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h2)

question: Chlorinating a community borehole to prevent waterborne disease targets which part of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Host
options.B: Agent
options.C: Environment
options.D: Vector

explanation: Improving water sources modifies external environmental conditions to prevent the transmission of pathogens to humans. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h2)

question: Which disease in Nigeria peaks primarily during the dry harmattan season in northern states?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Lassa fever
options.C: Meningococcal meningitis

question: The primary animal reservoir responsible for transmitting Lassa virus to humans is which of the following?

options.A: Cattle and goats
options.B: Multi-mammate rat
options.C: Mosquito vector
options.D: Domestic dog

explanation: Lassa fever is zoonotic, transmitted when humans come into contact with the excretions of the multi-mammate rat. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h3)

question: Drinking contaminated water during a community flood most directly transmits which type of infection?

options.A: Direct contact
options.B: Airborne
options.C: Vector-borne
options.D: Waterborne

question: Which factor most significantly increases the risk of spreading airborne infections like measles in a ward?

options.A: Overcrowding and poor ventilation
options.B: Drinking untreated borehole water
options.C: Eating unwashed fruits
options.D: Contact with rat droppings

explanation: Airborne pathogens spread easily when many people share a confined, poorly ventilated space where droplets linger. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h4)

question: What is the primary role of a primary health care nurse when an unusual cluster of symptoms appears?

options.A: Wait for national health officials to visit
options.B: Detect and report cases early
options.C: Treat patients privately without logging data
options.D: Immediately quarantine the entire local government area

explanation: Frontline nurses must identify unusual disease patterns and report them promptly to initiate public health responses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h5)

question: Why is gathering a detailed travel and contact history crucial during a disease outbreak assessment?

options.A: It replaces the need for laboratory testing of body fluids

options.C: It determines the exact financial cost of patient treatment
options.D: It proves whether the patient received childhood immunizations

explanation: Contact and travel histories reveal where the patient contracted the pathogen, aiding epidemiological tracking and containment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h5)

question: What intervention involves monitoring individuals who have been exposed to a confirmed contagious patient?

options.A: Mass deworming
options.B: Herd immunity
options.C: Contact tracing
options.D: Environmental sanitation

explanation: Contact tracing identifies and tracks people exposed to an infection to monitor symptoms and prevent further spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h6)

question: Why is personal protective equipment essential when nursing a patient with a suspected viral hemorrhagic fever?

options.A: To keep the patient comfortable during routine bed baths

options.C: To shield the nurse from breathing airborne dust particles
options.D: To prevent direct contact with infectious body fluids

explanation: Viral hemorrhagic fevers spread through contact with infected blood and body fluids, making barrier protection vital for staff safety. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h6)

question: How should a nurse approach health education in a rural community during a disease outbreak?

options.A: Rely entirely on written pamphlets without verbal explanation

options.C: Focus only on hospital-based patients ignoring the community
options.D: Use local languages and address cultural beliefs

explanation: Effective communication requires using familiar languages and addressing local myths to ensure behavior change. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core community nursing responsibility during an active epidemic?

options.A: Conducting contact tracing within affected neighborhoods
options.B: Diagnosing and prescribing new pharmaceutical drugs independently
options.C: Providing health education on hand hygiene and sanitation
options.D: Supporting psychological needs of stigmatized families

explanation: Independent diagnosis and prescribing of novel drugs fall outside standard nursing scope, whereas education, contact tracing, and support are core nursing duties. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of disease control in public health?

options.A: Eliminating the need for routine vaccination campaigns
options.B: Reducing disease incidence and mortality to acceptable levels
options.C: Isolating every infected patient in a national hospital
options.D: Completely removing all pathogens from the human body

explanation: Disease control focuses on lowering the burden of illness to manageable public health thresholds. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h1)

question: Why does public health practice prioritize interrupting transmission chains over individual treatment?

options.A: Individual hospital treatment is too expensive for government
options.B: Stopping spread protects the wider community from infection
options.C: Patients refuse to take medications prescribed by nurses
options.D: Pathogens cannot survive outside a single human host

explanation: Interrupted transmission prevents new cases from occurring in the population at large. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h1)

question: What term describes the constant presence of a disease in a specific geographic area?

options.A: Epidemic
options.B: Sporadic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Pandemic

explanation: An endemic disease maintains a predictable, steady baseline presence within a region. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h2)

question: A sudden surge of cholera cases in a state where it rarely occurs is best classified as what?

options.A: A prevalence
options.B: An eradication
options.C: An epidemic
options.D: An endemic

explanation: An unexpected rise above normal baseline levels in a specific area is an epidemic. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h2)

question: What defines the complete global reduction of a specific disease to zero cases?

options.A: Elimination
options.B: Suppression
options.C: Containment
options.D: Eradication

explanation: Eradication means the pathogen no longer exists anywhere on earth naturally. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h3)

question: Why must a country maintain vaccination programs even after achieving regional elimination of a disease?

options.A: Eliminated diseases always return within exactly one year
options.B: Imported cases from other areas can restart transmission
options.C: Local pathogens mutate spontaneously inside healthy people
options.D: Global health organizations force countries to buy vaccines

explanation: Porous borders allow pathogens to cross back into regions that previously achieved elimination. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h3)

question: Which intervention is a classic example of primary disease prevention?

options.A: Treating an active typhoid infection
options.B: Screening for high blood pressure
options.C: Routine childhood immunization
options.D: Physiotherapy for stroke patients

explanation: Immunization stops disease before it ever starts, which defines primary prevention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h4)

question: A community nurse organizing blood pressure screening at a market square is practicing which level of prevention?

options.A: Secondary prevention
options.B: Tertiary prevention
options.C: Primary prevention
options.D: Quaternary prevention

explanation: Screening detects existing hidden disease early so treatment can start before complications develop. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of a public health surveillance system?

options.A: Collecting and analyzing health data to guide interventions
options.B: Punishing clinics that fail to report patient admissions
options.C: Conducting laboratory research on new pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Providing free medications to chronically ill patients

explanation: Surveillance gathers data continuously to detect trends and direct public health actions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h5)

question: A clinic nurse notices an unusual cluster of watery diarrhea and immediately reports it through official channels. What system is being utilized?

options.A: Tertiary rehabilitation
options.B: Health promotion
options.C: Primary immunization
options.D: Disease surveillance

explanation: Reporting unusual clusters of symptoms is a core component of active disease surveillance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h5)

question: What is the first logical step when health authorities suspect a disease outbreak?

options.A: Destroying local water supply infrastructure
options.B: Closing all schools and public markets
options.C: Ordering millions of vaccines from abroad
options.D: Confirming the existence of the outbreak

explanation: Investigators must first verify that reported cases exceed normal baseline expectancy before launching a full response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h6)

question: During an outbreak investigation, why do epidemiologists analyze cases by time, place, and person?

options.A: To identify the source and mode of disease transmission
options.B: To write history books about past infectious diseases
options.C: To determine how much money the government should spend
options.D: To prove that nurses are working hard in rural clinics

explanation: Descriptive epidemiology maps out patterns that reveal where and how the pathogen is spreading. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h6)

question: Which activity is a direct nursing responsibility in community disease control?

options.A: Funding international public health research grants
options.B: Passing national laws on environmental sanitation
options.C: Administering vaccines during outreach programs
options.D: Manufacturing antibiotics in national pharmaceutical plants

explanation: Nurses directly deliver preventative services such as immunizations directly to community members. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h7)

question: Why do community nurses work closely with traditional or religious leaders during disease control campaigns?

options.A: To build local trust and encourage community participation
options.B: To diagnose complex viral infections without a laboratory
options.C: To receive financial donations for the local health clinic
options.D: To enforce strict police arrests for non-compliant citizens

explanation: Engaging respected community leaders helps overcome hesitation and improves public cooperation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h7)

question: What is the primary aim of disease prevention measures in public health?

options.B: Stopping disease onset and reducing illness effects
options.C: Focusing solely on curative hospital treatments
options.D: Building more advanced tertiary care hospitals

explanation: Disease prevention focuses on stopping the onset and halting the progression of illnesses before they require heavy curative care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h1)

question: Why does public health nursing emphasize prevention over treatment?

options.B: Patients prefer staying at home instead of hospitals
options.C: Government funding only allows preventive programs
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any medications

explanation: Shifting focus to prevention reduces the strain on healthcare facilities by addressing determinants like sanitation and nutrition early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h1)

question: Distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets to stop malaria exposure represents which level of prevention?

options.A: Tertiary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Secondary prevention
options.D: Primordial prevention

explanation: Primary prevention involves protecting healthy individuals from specific disease agents before exposure happens. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h2)

question: How does primordial prevention differ from primary prevention?

options.A: Primordial occurs after disease onset while primary happens before
options.B: Primordial is only used in hospitals while primary is community-based
options.C: Primordial treats chronic symptoms while primary provides vaccines
options.D: Primordial targets broad social policies while primary targets specific risk factors

explanation: Primordial prevention addresses broad social and environmental conditions, whereas primary prevention acts against specific agents and known risk factors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h2)

question: Physiotherapy for a patient recovering from a stroke is an example of which level?

options.A: Secondary prevention
options.B: Primordial prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Primary prevention

question: A community nurse organizing routine blood pressure screening aims primarily to achieve what outcome?

question: What type of immunity is conferred through routine childhood vaccinations?

options.A: Artificial passive immunity
options.B: Active immunity
options.C: Innate immunity
options.D: Natural passive immunity

question: Why is intermittent preventive treatment for malaria administered to pregnant women in endemic areas?

question: What characteristic of a screening test ensures it correctly identifies individuals without the disease?

question: What is the necessary next step after a patient screens positive for a chronic illness?

question: Which approach is most essential for the long-term sustainability of community disease control programs?

question: Why must health education campaigns be tailored to local cultural contexts?

explanation: Culturally relevant education respects local beliefs and increases the likelihood of positive behavior modification. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h6)

question: What is a primary clinical responsibility of community health nurses in prevention programs?

options.A: Performing major surgical operations in field hospitals

options.D: Determining national healthcare budgetary allocations

question: How do nurses bridge the gap between national health policies and rural communities?

options.B: By replacing traditional healers with certified medical doctors
options.C: By restricting healthcare access to insured urban residents
options.D: By translating public health goals into grassroots educational activities

question: What happens when microorganisms develop resistance to standard antimicrobial drugs?

options.A: The infectious agents turn into beneficial normal flora
options.B: The pathogens become completely harmless to humans
options.C: The drugs become completely ineffective against them
options.D: The microbes multiply much slower in the host

explanation: Resistant microorganisms develop mechanisms to survive treatments that previously killed them, rendering standard drugs useless. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h1)

question: Why is antimicrobial resistance considered a natural evolutionary process?

options.A: Chemicals in modern drugs make bacteria permanently immortal
options.B: Pathogens mutate and adapt to survive environmental pressures
options.C: Microbes choose to become stronger to attack human hosts
options.D: Human immune systems train pathogens to resist medications

explanation: Microbes naturally undergo genetic changes to survive threats in their environment, and drug exposure speeds up this survival selection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h1)

question: What is the primary function of bacterial efflux pumps in drug resistance?

options.A: Destroying the drug molecules using special enzymes
options.B: Altering the target binding sites of the medication
options.C: Pumping the antimicrobial drug out of the cell
options.D: Modifying the cell wall to block drug entry

explanation: Efflux pumps act as microscopic security guards, actively pushing the drug out before it can harm the bacterium. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h2)

question: How do beta-lactamase enzymes protect bacteria from penicillin-class drugs?

options.A: By chemically destroying the active molecule of the antibiotic
options.B: By flushing the medication out through active transport
options.C: By tricking the immune system into attacking the drug
options.D: By sealing the cell membrane so the drug cannot enter

explanation: Beta-lactamases break down the chemical structure of the drug, making it harmless to the bacterial cell. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h2)

question: What defines innate resistance in a microorganism?

options.A: It develops after repeated exposure to strong antibiotics
options.B: It is a natural, inherent trait present from the beginning
options.C: It is acquired through horizontal gene transfer from peers
options.D: It occurs due to a spontaneous mutation during illness

explanation: Innate resistance is built into the normal biology of the organism without requiring any prior exposure to drugs or genetic mutation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h3)

question: How does acquired resistance typically spread rapidly among different bacterial species?

options.D: By natural changes in the patient's normal body temperature

question: Which practice directly contributes to resistance within human medicine?

question: Why does using sub-therapeutic doses of antimicrobials in livestock promote resistance?

question: Why do routine medical procedures like surgery become dangerous when resistance is widespread?

question: What is a direct clinical consequence for patients infected with resistant pathogens?

question: What is considered the single most effective barrier against cross-contamination in clinical settings?

question: A patient wants to stop taking their prescribed antibiotics because the fever has stopped. What is the nurse's best action?

question: What best describes disease surveillance in public health?

question: What characterizes passive surveillance in a health system?

options.C: Exactly 25 micrometers
options.D: 5 micrometers or smaller

explanation: Pathogens causing airborne infections travel inside tiny droplet nuclei that measure 5 micrometers or less, allowing them to stay suspended in the air. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Why do airborne pathogens travel much further than typical respiratory droplets?

options.A: They actively swim through the atmosphere toward warm-blooded hosts.
options.B: They are propelled forward by high-velocity mechanical fans in wards.
options.C: They evaporate and remain suspended in air currents as tiny nuclei.
options.D: They bind to heavy dust particles that carry them across long distances.

explanation: Droplet nuclei undergo partial evaporation, leaving light, microscopic cores that can drift on air currents far beyond the immediate proximity of the patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Where in the respiratory tract do tiny droplet nuclei typically settle after inhalation?

options.A: Mainstem bronchi
options.B: Terminal alveoli
options.C: Nasal turbinates
options.D: Pharyngeal mucosa

explanation: Because of their extremely small size, droplet nuclei bypass upper airway defenses and travel deep into the terminal alveoli of the lungs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: What environmental condition most directly increases the concentration of airborne pathogens indoors?

options.A: High ultraviolet lighting
options.B: Poor room ventilation
options.C: Excessive floor washing
options.D: Low ambient temperature

explanation: Enclosed spaces lacking proper air exchange trap infectious aerosols, increasing the viral or bacterial load in the environment and raising infection risk. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: Which clinical sign is most characteristic of measles infection?

options.A: Koplik spots
options.B: Productive bloody sputum
options.C: Jaundiced sclera
options.D: Painful neck stiffness

explanation: Koplik spots appearing on the buccal mucosa are a classic early diagnostic sign of measles before the rash appears. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: A patient presents with a chronic cough lasting over four weeks, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. Which disease is most likely suspected?

options.A: Pulmonary tuberculosis
options.B: Acute malaria fever
options.C: Uncomplicated typhoid
options.D: Simple tension headache

explanation: Persistent cough lasting weeks alongside systemic signs like night sweats and weight loss points strongly toward active pulmonary tuberculosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: What is a primary clinical finding during the physical assessment of a patient with severe pulmonary infection?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles
options.B: Generalized skin pallor
options.C: Absent bowel sounds
options.D: Bounding peripheral pulses

explanation: Respiratory distress forces the body to recruit accessory muscles of the neck and chest to assist with labored breathing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: Why is early pulse oximetry monitoring essential during the assessment of respiratory infections?

options.A: It measures the exact bacterial load circulating in the bloodstream.
options.B: It detects developing hypoxemia before overt cyanosis appears.
options.C: It determines the patient's exact daily fluid intake requirements.
options.D: It diagnoses the specific causative organism without lab tests.

explanation: Pulse oximetry provides an objective measurement of blood oxygen saturation, revealing hypoxia long before visible skin color changes like cyanosis occur. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: What laboratory test provides rapid detection of tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance?

options.A: GeneXpert MTB/RIF
options.B: Widal agglutination test
options.C: Full blood count profile
options.D: Urinalysis reagent strip

explanation: GeneXpert is a molecular diagnostic tool that rapidly detects tuberculosis DNA and identifies resistance to rifampicin within hours. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of ordering a chest radiograph for a patient with a suspected airborne lung infection?

options.A: To culture the specific bacterial species causing the infection
options.B: To visualize infiltrates, cavities, or consolidation in the lung tissue
options.C: To evaluate the electrical conduction system of the heart muscle
options.D: To measure the exact oxygen saturation level inside the alveoli

explanation: Imaging studies like chest X-rays allow clinicians to see structural lung changes such as cavities or consolidation typical of severe infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: What type of room ventilation is specifically required for patients with suspected active airborne infections?

options.A: Positive pressure surgical suite
options.B: Standard natural draft ward
options.C: Sealed hyperbaric oxygen chamber
options.D: Negative pressure isolation room

explanation: Negative pressure rooms prevent contaminated air from escaping into hallways when doors are opened by pulling air inward through specialized exhaust systems. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: Why is strict adherence to medication schedules critical in the management of bacterial airborne infections like tuberculosis?

options.A: It prevents treatment failure and the emergence of drug-resistant strains.
options.B: It reduces the financial cost of hospital admission for the family.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any subsequent laboratory investigations.
options.D: It immediately stops the patient from coughing within two hours.

explanation: Skipping doses or erratic drug intake allows surviving pathogens to mutate and develop resistance, making future infections much harder to treat. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: Which type of personal protective equipment must nurses wear when caring for patients with confirmed airborne diseases?

options.A: N95 respirator mask
options.B: Heavy industrial dust mask
options.C: Standard paper surgical mask
options.D: Clear plastic face shield only

explanation: N95 respirators create a tight facial seal and filter out microscopic airborne droplet nuclei, unlike loose-fitting surgical masks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of administrative IPC controls in a primary healthcare clinic?

options.A: Conducting chemical disinfection of hospital linen daily
options.B: Procuring high-cost ventilators for intensive care units
options.C: Providing free meals to all admitted infectious patients
options.D: Promptly identifying and separating coughing patients at triage

explanation: Administrative controls focus on early recognition and separation of potentially infectious individuals before they expose others in waiting areas. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)

question: What is a core component of proper cough etiquette taught during public health campaigns?

options.A: Covering the mouth and nose with the flexed elbow
options.B: Turning the head downward toward bare carpet flooring
options.C: Sputtering directly into open palms for hand washing later
options.D: Wearing thick leather gloves while speaking outdoors

explanation: Using the flexed elbow prevents respiratory droplets from contaminating hands and subsequent environmental surfaces. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h8)

question: Why is community engagement regarding airborne infections important in primary healthcare?

options.A: It stops seasonal weather changes from affecting respiratory health.
options.B: It replaces the need for clinical laboratories in remote villages.
options.C: It reduces social stigma and encourages early reporting of symptoms.
options.D: It guarantees immediate government funding for hospital infrastructure.

explanation: Engaging the community builds trust, dispels harmful myths, and empowers individuals to seek diagnosis early before complications arise. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h8)

question: What is a fomite in the context of contact infections?

options.A: An insect vector that transmits tropical diseases
options.B: A specialized white blood cell fighting bacteria
options.C: A chemical used to sterilize surgical instruments
options.D: A non-living object that harbors infectious agents

explanation: Fomites are inanimate surfaces or objects like door handles and shared clothing that transfer pathogens between hosts. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h1)

question: Indirect contact transmission differs from direct contact because it involves what?

options.A: Blood-sucking vectors like mosquitoes and ticks
options.B: Airborne droplet nuclei traveling long distances
options.C: Ingestion of contaminated municipal water supplies
options.D: An intermediate non-living object or surface

explanation: Indirect spread relies on fomites to bridge the physical gap between the infected source and the new host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h1)

question: Scabies is a classic example of which type of transmission?

options.A: Common vehicle transmission
options.B: Direct contact transmission
options.C: Airborne droplet transmission
options.D: Vector-borne transmission

explanation: Scabies mites burrow into the skin and transfer directly from one person's skin to another during close contact. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h2)

question: Why is environmental surface cleaning vital for controlling indirect contact infections?

options.A: Cleaning prevents vectors from breeding inside hospital wards
options.B: Pathogens survive on fomites and wait for a new host
options.C: Chemical disinfectants destroy airborne spores instantly
options.D: Wiping surfaces stops droplet nuclei from spreading further

explanation: Indirect infections spread because germs linger on inanimate objects, making regular disinfection necessary to break the chain. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h2)

question: Which bacterium is most commonly responsible for skin boils and wound infections?

options.A: Salmonella typhi
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Escherichia coli
options.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus lives on human skin and frequently causes purulent soft tissue infections and boils. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h3)

question: What environmental condition in tropical regions encourages the spread of fungal skin infections?

options.A: Low atmospheric pressure at high altitudes
options.B: Consistent cold weather during harmattan
options.C: High humidity and warm temperatures
options.D: Prolonged exposure to dry desert winds

explanation: Fungi flourish in warm and moist environments, making tropical climates ideal for dermatophyte growth and skin irritation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h3)

question: Why does scabies infestation cause intense itching, especially at night?

options.A: Fungal spores releasing histamines into the bloodstream
options.B: Allergic reactions to burrowed mites and their waste
options.C: Viral replication peaking during dark hours
options.D: Bacterial toxins destroying deep muscle tissues

explanation: The body mounts an immune response against the protein waste and eggs left by mites under the skin, causing severe pruritus. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h4)

question: A patient with a primary fungal skin infection develops pus and increased pain. What has likely happened?

options.A: The fungus has transformed into a virus
options.B: Normal systemic reaction to anti-fungal drugs
options.C: Secondary bacterial infection from scratching
options.D: Spontaneous healing of the original lesion

explanation: Breaking the skin barrier through scratching allows resident skin bacteria like staphylococci to enter and cause secondary infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h4)

question: What bedside procedure helps confirm a suspected fungal skin infection?

options.A: Complete blood count with differential analysis
options.B: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) skin scraping preparation
options.C: Chest X-ray to check for pulmonary infiltrates
options.D: Urinalysis using a standard reagent strip

explanation: Treating skin scrapings with KOH dissolves keratinocytes and leaves fungal elements visible under microscopic examination. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h5)

question: Why is a wound swab for culture and sensitivity ordered before starting antibiotics?

options.A: To determine how long the patient has been sick
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of hospital admission
options.C: To identify the exact pathogen and effective drugs
options.D: To measure the patient's red blood cell volume

explanation: Culture and sensitivity testing pinpoints the causative microorganism and reveals which specific antimicrobial agents will cure the infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h5)

question: Which medication is standard first-line treatment for a scabies infestation?

options.A: Paracetamol syrup
options.B: Amoxicillin capsules
options.C: Hydrocortisone ointment
options.D: Permethrin cream

explanation: Permethrin is a safe and effective topical scabicide that kills both the mites and their eggs when applied correctly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h6)

question: What non-pharmacological step is essential when treating a family member for scabies?

options.A: Washing all shared bed linen and clothes in hot water
options.B: Stopping all fluid intake for twenty-four hours
options.C: Isolating the infected person in a dark room for a month
options.D: Applying heavy makeup over the affected skin lesions

explanation: Mites can survive briefly on fabrics, so laundering clothing and bedding in hot water prevents immediate reinfection from fomites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h6)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop cross-contamination in healthcare settings?

options.A: Wearing sterile face masks all day
options.B: Spraying corridors with strong disinfectants
options.C: Restricting all visitors from the ward
options.D: Frequent and proper hand hygiene

explanation: Handwashing or using alcohol rub removes transient microorganisms acquired from patients and contaminated surfaces. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h7)

question: Which personal protective equipment is required when entering a room under contact precautions?

options.A: Gloves and gowns
options.B: N95 respirator only
options.C: Rubber boots and apron
options.D: Face shield and cap

explanation: Contact precautions require barriers like gloves and gowns to prevent direct skin contact with the patient and contaminated environmental surfaces. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h7)

question: Why should nurses engage local community leaders when planning public health campaigns?

options.A: To secure direct financial grants from international donors
options.B: To gain local trust and encourage community participation
options.C: To punish families who refuse to follow medical advice
options.D: To bypass government health policies and protocols

explanation: Community leaders hold influence and help bridge the gap between healthcare workers and local residents, ensuring better acceptance of health education. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h8)

question: Which educational message is most important for preventing the spread of fungal ringworm in schools?

options.A: Take strong oral antibiotics every morning
options.B: Wear heavy woolen sweaters in hot weather
options.C: Avoid sharing personal items like combs and towels
options.D: Wash hands only after eating meals

explanation: Fungal skin and scalp infections spread easily through shared grooming tools, hats, and clothing among school children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h8)
